title: Concurrent optimization of capital cost and expected o&m
contribution: NREL project report on design and O&M optimization of molten-salt power towers; its optimization-methods section proposes a mixed-integer derivative-free method that minimizes a MILP-encoded secant underestimator over integer points, with valid big-M/lambda constants, useful-point heuristics and an l-infinity trust region on the integers.
problem_entry: Plant design minimizing PPA price is a mixed-integer, derivative-free problem under uncertainty (black-box SAM simulation of several minutes, expectation over weather and prices); model-based MINLP methods need algebraic functions and DFO methods assume deterministic continuous problems (pp. 15-19).
key_idea: Piecewise-linear underestimator from secant hyperplanes through poised sets of n+1 evaluated integer points, minimized by a MILP master; tightened constants, useful-point heuristics, and an l-infinity trust region enlarged only when the model is infeasible; continuous subproblem at each integer point solved by BOBYQA/COBYLA (pp. 19-25).
assumptions: Constraints are bounds on x with simulation constraints folded into the objective (p. 16); expectation risk measure (p. 18); a valid lower bound l_f on the bounded integer domain (p. 20).
proof_devices: Integral-hyperplane lattice distance >= 1/||c||_2 gives a valid lambda (Proposition 3.2.1, p. 21)
Minimal-||c||_1 integral hyperplane through n points found by a small IP (P-hyp), then constants tightened by per-hyperplane optimization (eqs. 3.5-3.7, pp. 20-21)
No-good cuts or a binary-expanded valid inequality to stop repeated iterates (p. 21)
Global convergence of the trust-region variant asserted, not proved in the text read (p. 23)
experiments: Benchmark at n = 2-4: gap and wall-clock time with and without trust region; CPLEX master times out at n = 3, enumeration at n = 4 (Figs. 6-7, p. 24); one-at-a-time plant parameter studies with 15-20% PPA/LCOE improvement (pp. 109-110).
positioning: Three solution classes for simulation-based mixed-integer design (evolutionary, pattern search, model-based); chooses model-based because it supports a posteriori sensitivity analysis; cites OA, GBD, ECP, Minotaur, Bonmin as inapplicable to non-algebraic functions (p. 18).
writing: Project-report register: numbered deliverables, limits stated as flat verdicts (pp. 19, 112); no per-author attribution of sections in the text (pp. 4, 13).
limits_future: Constant tightening does not make the master a competitive subproblem solver; useful points sometimes hard to find; model creation remains the bottleneck (p. 19); scatter in optimized designs needs better constraints and convergence criteria (p. 111); future: more market cases, data, public software (p. 112).

method_links.note: Trust region plus MILP master carried from the MINLP/NLP toolkit into mixed-integer simulation-based DFO; Leyffer's authorship of this section is inferred, not stated
Valid big-M and lambda constants derived so the master stays a lower bound before speed-ups
Limits stated plainly; CPLEX and enumeration baselines shown timing out

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: l-infinity trust region on integer variables in a cutting-plane DFO method, radius increased only when the model is infeasible (also S065)

transferable: Get lambda for a big-M secant-underestimator MILP from the lattice distance 1/||c||_2 of an integral hyperplane, then tighten it by a small optimization problem per hyperplane (p. 21).
In a cutting-plane method over integer points, enlarge the l-infinity trust region only when the model inside it is infeasible; take null steps otherwise (Algorithm 1, p. 23).
Measure which cuts actually prune a promising point (useful cuts and points) before designing a cut-selection heuristic (Figs. 4-5, p. 22).
coauthors: Michael J. Wagner, Alexandra Newman, David Morton; 13 listed contributors including Jeffrey Larson (pp. 1, 4)

quotes.text: Traditional derivative-free optimization techniques are designed for problems with deterministic simulations and continuous variables.
Tightening these bounds improves the solution time, but not to the level that makes it a competitive sub-problem solver.

title: Wave function analysis with a maximum flow algorithm
contribution: A max-min flow recursion with backtracking, density removal and a greedy fallback extracts the dominant CSFs of a graphically contracted wave function from arc densities alone, at cost independent of the CSF dimension, with a certified top-M' partition; demonstrated on three C2 states.
problem_entry: GCF wave functions can have N_CSF > 10^200, so scanning all CSF coefficients is impractical, but arc densities on the Shavitt graph are cheap to compute (pp. 4-5).
key_idea: Shavitt graph as a flow network with arc densities as capacities; level-ordered d_k = max_j min(d_j, rho_jk) bounds the largest walk density per node, backtracking gives a candidate walk, its density is removed and the process repeats; heap-ranked greedy deviation search when candidates repeat (pp. 6-9).
assumptions: Arc densities available; candidate guaranteed correct only when its density exceeds half the unsaved density (Eq. 6, p. 7); one-dimensional irreps of D2h and subgroups (p. 10).
proof_devices: Max-min recursion yields upper bounds on the walk density through each node (p. 7)
Monotone bounds d_head and d_tail partition generated walks into a certified top-M' set and an undetermined rest (p. 9)
Four-CSF worked example and a one-parameter family x(s) showing a wrong first extraction, self-correction, and many-to-one maps (pp. 18-19)
experiments: One proof-of-principle: three valence states of C2 dissociation (6-31G*), compared with literature full-CI curves; seven dominant CSFs analysed (pp. 11-17).
positioning: Positioned against scanning and sorting the full CSF list and against approximate wave functions from reduced spaces, which can introduce artifacts (p. 5).
writing: Chemistry-journal register; heuristic step openly labelled ad hoc (pp. 8-9); failure case worked out in an appendix (pp. 18-19).
limits_future: Extraction order can be wrong and the greedy step is ad hoc (pp. 7-9); future extension to DMRG and coupled-cluster expansions (p. 18).

method_links.note: Smallest example on which the method extracts the wrong walk is built, run and explained; weak evidence because the paper is chemist-led and Leyffer's role is unstated
Network-flow optimization device carried into a quantum-chemistry object; weak, role unstated

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: certify part of a heuristic's output with monotone bounds
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Upper bounds on all unextracted walks certify which generated walks are truly among the largest

transferable: When a greedy extraction cannot guarantee order, maintain a monotone upper bound on everything not yet extracted and report only the items above it as certified (p. 9).
State the exact sufficient condition under which the greedy step is correct (majority of the remaining mass) and give a small worked example where it fails (pp. 7, 18-19).
coauthors: Ron Shepard, Scott R. Brozell, Jeffrey Larson, Paul Hovland

quotes.text: the dominant CSFs are generated, but not necessarily in the correct order, and in this sense the algorithm has some capacity to self-correct.
No step in this novel procedure requires effort or storage that scales as NCSF, and the algorithm is applicable to wave function expansions of practically arbitrary size.

title: Modeling design and control problems involving neural network surrogates: D. Yang et al.
contribution: Shows that embedding trained ReLU networks directly in NLPs converges poorly, characterizes stationarity of that embedded model, and compares two lifted reformulations (convex MINLP via big-M, and an MPCC solved as an NLP, proved stationarity-equivalent) with training-data warm starts and convex-hull constraints on three applications (read as arXiv v1).
problem_entry: Optimization over trained ReLU surrogates, min f(DNN(x),x) s.t. c(DNN(x),x) <= 0; entered from the observation that Ipopt fails to converge on the embedded formulation, with dual infeasibility staying high (pp. 1, 9).
key_idea: Lift the network: one binary per ReLU gives a convex MINLP when f, c, X are convex (Proposition 4); complementarity 0 <= y perp s >= 0 with slacks and y^T s <= 0 gives an NLP-solvable MPCC; plus convex-hull-of-training-data constraints and a training-data warm start (pp. 4-6, 14-16).
assumptions: f, c C2 and convex, X convex compact (Assumption 1, p. 2), convexity called the most restrictive; trained, fixed network (p. 2); general position of activation hyperplanes for Theorems 1-2 (pp. 12-13).
proof_devices: Clarke generalized Jacobian of a piecewise-linear ReLU network as a convex hull of masked weight-matrix products under general position (Propositions 2-3, pp. 12-13)
KKT-type stationarity conditions for the embedded model (Theorem 1, p. 13)
Equivalence of embedded stationarity and MPCC strong stationarity via multiplier scaling factors (Proposition 5, Theorem 2, p. 16)
Per-neuron bound-tightening problems for big-M constants (p. 14)
experiments: CPLEX (MIP) and Ipopt (MPCC, embedded) at default options, single thread; engine design over 1/3/5-layer nets and time grids, 100 MNIST attacks on 10 architectures, oil-well networks with Bonmin; time to best, gap to best known, counts of optimal and feasible runs (pp. 16-21).
positioning: Builds on Fischetti-Jo and Anderson et al. big-M and ideal formulations; differs from Cheon's OA-inspired method by exploiting convexity after lifting; the MPCC side rests on Fletcher-Leyffer 2004 and Fletcher-Leyffer-Ralph-Scholtes 2006 (pp. 3, 13, 15).
writing: Each formulation gets an advantages-and-costs verdict, not a single winner (pp. 17-18, 22); an empirical failure motivates the theory section (pp. 9-10).
limits_future: MIP limited to about 100 hidden nodes (p. 14); MPCC only locally optimal (p. 15); embedded ReLU model converges poorly, swish suggested (p. 22); convex-hull constraint keeps solutions near the data (pp. 4-5); embedded model not runnable on the oil-well MINLP in JuMP (p. 20).

method_links.note: Solver log read first, a swish control run rules out the solver, formulation changed before any algorithm; convex-hull constraint repairs a negative-emissions model
ReLU networks recast as convex MINLP and as MPCC with his own slack formulation for complementarity
Same machine and failures counted, but solvers run at default options rather than at their best settings

transferable: When an NLP solver fails on a nonsmooth model, rerun with a smooth surrogate of the nonsmooth piece (swish for ReLU) to attribute the failure to the formulation rather than the solver (p. 10).
Constrain surrogate inputs to the convex hull of the training inputs and report what the unconstrained optimum looked like (p. 4).
Warm-start the lifted model from training data: pick constraint-satisfying training points of least cost and set every neuron variable to its activation there (Algorithm 1, pp. 5-6).
When proposing a reformulation of a nonsmooth model, prove that its stationary points coincide with those of the original (Theorem 2, p. 16).

quotes.text: In fact, in an earlier implementation without the convex hull constraint, we observed that the optimal design was obtained for an engine that produced negative emissions.
This observation makes the use of ReLU networks questionable as embedded constraints within optimization solvers that rely on differentiable problem functions.

title: Sequential linear integer programming for integer optimal control with total variation regularization
contribution: For TV-regularized integer optimal control, proves existence of minimizers, defines r-optimality in L1-neighbourhoods, and gives a function-space trust-region method with linear-IP subproblems (SLIP) whose iterates converge for d = 1 to L-stationary points; compared computationally with SCIP MIQP and CIA+SCARP (read as arXiv v3).
problem_entry: Combinatorial integral approximation gives oscillating controls whose TV goes to infinity, and its theory fails with a TV term; global solves of the discretized problem do not scale to fine meshes (p. 2).
key_idea: TV regularization yields minimizers; the trust-region subproblem linearizes F but keeps TV exact under an L1 radius and becomes a linear IP after DG0 discretization; reset-and-halve radius control with an ared/pred test (pp. 2-7).
assumptions: F lsc and bounded below (Assumption 2.1, p. 3); for convergence d = 1 and F C2 with Hessian bounded in L1 x L1 (Assumption 4.1, p. 8), satisfied by least squares with K: L1 -> L2 bounded (Proposition 4.2, p. 8) and used only for Taylor's theorem (Remark 4.16, p. 12).
proof_devices: BV boundedness, weak-* compactness and lower semicontinuity of TV for existence (Propositions 2.3, 3.2, pp. 3, 5)
Shrinking-ball construction showing every L1-neighbourhood of an integer control contains other feasible controls (Example 2.9, p. 4)
Auxiliary switching-location problem (L) and L-stationarity as the first-order condition (Theorem 4.14, p. 12)
TV of the iterates settles after finitely many steps, read as an active set settling down (Theorem 4.23, p. 14; Remark 4.26, p. 17)
experiments: 1-D convolution tracking with five control levels, N = 32-2048, SCIP 7.0; four SLIP variants, SLIP vs MIQP (5 h limit) vs CIA+SCARP, 25 random starts x 8 values of alpha, local MINLP check of r-optimality (pp. 19-25).
positioning: Contrasted with combinatorial integral approximation and its TV-aware rounding variants, with global solves of the discretized problem, and with a set-based method that lacks existence of stationary feasible points (p. 2).
writing: Contributions paragraph frames the method as an NLP trust-region analogue (p. 2); the conclusion reports where it loses before the future work (p. 26).
limits_future: MIQP better for N <= 128 and CIA better for N = 64, 128; computationally less attractive than CIA; analysis only for d = 1; faster doubling-radius variant unproved; future: use L-stationarity in the algorithm, adaptive grids, curvature, a rule for alpha (pp. 8, 19, 22, 26).

method_links.note: NLP trust-region globalization and active-set reasoning carried into integer optimal control in function space
Reports losses to SCIP MIQP and CIA; clips relative differences at the solver tolerance for a fair comparison

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: L1 trust region on integer-valued controls with linear-IP subproblems (also S146)

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: regularize until the integer problem has minimizers, then descend on the feasible set
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: TV term gives existence and lets the algorithm stay integer-feasible instead of relaxing and rounding

transferable: In an integer trust-region subproblem, linearize only the smooth part and keep the nonsmooth regularizer exact, so the subproblem stays a linear IP and pred compares directly with ared (pp. 5-7).

Before proving convergence for a discretized integer method, show by a shrinking-ball construction that the finite-dimensional local-minimizer notion is empty in the limit, and define a meaningful neighbourhood (Example 2.9, Definition 2.8, p. 4).
Check r-optimality a posteriori by re-solving the MINLP in a small L1-ball around the returned point and reporting the relative gap clipped at the solver tolerance (pp. 23-25).
Report both a proven variant and a faster unproven one, labelled as such (pp. 21, 26).

quotes.text: The topological restrictions induced by the discreteness constraint and the TV-regularizer are strong enough such that (P) admits optimal solutions.
However, the algorithmic framework is computationally less attractive than the combinatorial integral decomposition.
